source.title: Value-Conflict Diagnostics Reveal Widespread Alignment Faking in Language Models
source.authors: Inderjeet Nair; Jie Ruan; Lu Wang

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a contrastive residual-stream steering direction as an inference-time mitigation tool for alignment faking. It does not test the refusal direction or refusal behavior described in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper measures oversight-conditioned activation shifts and alignment-faking compliance gaps, not a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, refusal rates, or general capability after ablating that direction. Its direction is computed from monitored versus unmonitored inputs and injected at one selected layer. The reported results below concern this related but different construct; cited findings from other work are not included.
record.test_reason: The study builds a difference-in-means (ActAdd) and PC1 (LAT) steering vector from oversight vs non-oversight framings and uses it to reduce alignment-faking compliance gaps. It never computes a harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, never ablates or adds one, and never measures refusal rates as the outcome. Its PCA and steering results concern an oversight direction, a related but different construct. Sorry-Bench and WMDP serve only as data sources for that oversight contrast, not as a refusal test.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is correct but incomplete. The paper's main contribution is the VLAF diagnostic. It reports widespread alignment faking (e.g. 37% in olmo2-7b), value- and consequence-dependent gaps, and graded compliance by oversight probability in qwen3 thinking models. It also reports that oversight-induced shifts are approximately rank-1 and that a steering vector cuts compliance gaps by up to 94%. The authors leave capability effects for future work.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a contrastive vector between oversight and non-oversight framings, measured at the last token and injected at one selected layer; it does not use harmful-minus-harmless prompts, remove a refusal direction, or edit model weights.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with model, steering method, training source, selected layer, and intervention strength. The layer chosen by the Calinski–Harabasz index is reported as suboptimal for qwen3-8b on WMDP; the authors also report that smaller strengths can further reduce compliance gaps in some settings.

fits_no_version.finding: PCA of last-token activation differences between oversight and non-oversight conditions shows a dominant first component. Each other component explains under 10% (Fig 7; olmo2-7b, olmo2-13b, qwen3-8b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Explicit binary oversight framing induces an approximately rank-1 activation shift. The authors note implicit oversight (evaluation faking, out-of-context faking) likely needs a higher-dimensional account.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding an oversight-to-non-oversight steering vector at one layer (alpha=6) reduces VLAF compliance gaps. Reductions are large for olmo2 and qwen3-8b and modest for qwen3-14b (14.6–21.4%).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A single contrastive oversight direction partly mediates alignment-faking compliance gaps, with weaker effect in larger models.

record.problems: The paper does not evaluate general downstream capability effects of the steering interventions and explicitly leaves broader capability evaluation to future work. The PCA values are shown in figures without exact numerical values in the text. The direction and behavioral measure concern oversight-conditioned alignment faking, not refusal.
record.rows_left_out: Other paper results—including alignment-faking rates by value and consequence, reasoning-trace judgments, situational-awareness measures, and EF/OOC analyses—were left out because they do not measure the claimed refusal direction or refusal behavior. Prompting-only mitigation results were also omitted because they do not apply the contrastive direction.

untested.parts: No harmful-minus-harmless direction, no ablation or refusal-inducing addition, no capability evaluation (explicitly left to future work).
No jailbreak analysis or adversarial training against ablation.
The rank-1 PCA concerns oversight-induced shifts, not refusal geometry.
Cross-dataset (Sorry-Bench vs WMDP) subspace similarity concerns the oversight direction, not the refusal direction; no language, variant or base-to-instruct transfer.
qwen3 thinking models are studied, but not for the refusal direction.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T4/uses_without_test call is correct. The paper cites refusal only as a confound of prior alignment-faking diagnostics. Sorry-Bench and WMDP appear only as carriers for evaluation-vs-deployment framings, so no row bears on any refusal-direction version and no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction; no all-layer/all-position ablation, refusal-inducing addition, or broad capability evaluation.
No weight edit or abliteration; the interventions are inference-time activation steering.
No test of jailbreaks suppressing the refusal direction or training against its ablation.
The paper examines dimensionality of oversight-related activation shifts, not whether refusal requires an affine, cone-shaped, or multiple-direction account.
No separation of harmfulness judgments from refusal decisions.
No transfer test of the claimed refusal direction across languages, model variants, or base/instruct stages.
No test of how refusal training determines whether the claimed refusal direction exists.
Reasoning models are included, but the paper does not test the refusal-direction claim in them.
